talks.title: Hardware Hacking a Car’s Head Unit & Uncovering a Vulnerable RTOS,Danilo Erazo
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Hardware Hacking a Car’s Head Unit & Uncovering a Vulnerable RTOS,Danilo Erazo.
talks.summary:
Overview: Danilo Erazo travels from Ecuador to present at Hardwear.io USA on hardware hacking Kia automotive head units and discovering an undocumented real-time operating system.

Key Topics: Kia infotainment system architecture supplied by Mobis; the TMFM92000 system-on-chip with no public datasheet; flash memory and microcontroller components; and ongoing automotive cybersecurity research.

Technical Details: Erazo identifies the TMFM92000 SoC, WB25Q128 flash, and Renesas M16C microcontroller in Kia head units, noting zero public documentation on the primary processor. He invites researchers to contribute to this emerging RTOS analysis.

Takeaways: Automotive head units run undocumented RTOS platforms with minimal public security research. The car hacking community needs collaborative effort to map and secure these systems.

talks.title: Panel: How Research Influences Product Security
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Panel: How Research Influences Product Security.
talks.summary:
Panel Scope and Participants

A Hardwear IO panel moderated by co-founder Aim Jakar examines how independent security research influences hardware product security. Nolan Johnson represents the research community; Nir, Jason Meltzer, and Tamara Schmidtz represent product-security roles at Winbond, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, and Micron.

Reporting Friction

Panelists describe internal challenges when vulnerabilities surface—deciding whom to notify, triaging across chipset vendors versus OEMs, and navigating geographic and organizational barriers. Researchers note thoughtful choices about disclosure targets after findings such as Amlogic fault-injection issues.

Competitive and Cultural Tensions

Product teams acknowledge cybersecurity must be embedded across development, yet some vendors treat fixes as marketing—patching internally while competitors sharing the same silicon remain exposed. The relationship between researchers and vendors is described as bittersweet but necessary for safer products.

Improving the Relationship

Recommendations include executive education on security risk, accepting that risk cannot always be quantified cleanly, and building processes that welcome external research rather than treating it as adversarial noise.

talks.title: Smart Security: Protecting Embedded Medical Devices For A Safer Tomorrow
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Smart Security: Protecting Embedded Medical Devices For A Safer Tomorrow.
talks.summary:
Healthcare IoT Panel Introduction

Health-ISAC moderator Phil Angler hosts practitioners from Intuitive Surgical, Insulet, Somerset Recon, and Kaiser Permanente on securing embedded medical devices where patients—not just data—are in the threat path. Panelists span surgical robotics, insulin pumps, penetration testing, and health-system deployment.

Patient-Researcher Origins

Jay Radcliffe describes reverse-engineering his own Medtronic and Animas insulin pumps, talks that helped push FDA attention toward device cybersecurity. As a lifelong type-1 diabetic and now Insulet product security officer, he emphasizes life-safety stakes for devices keeping family members alive.

Hospital Defender Challenges

Kaiser Permanente's Michael Nguyen explains tailoring security controls per device type, partnering with manufacturers, validating implementations in limited test environments, and carefully deploying changes without disrupting clinical workflows. Costly devices and constant clinical use make comprehensive lab replicas difficult.

FDA Authority and Manufacturer Response

Congress granted FDA statutory cybersecurity authority in 2022 beyond traditional safety reviews. Intuitive's Melton Osoy details how Da Vinci surgical robot teams map FDA guidance to authentication, authorization, secure firmware update, and logging requirements for submissions, while hospitals increasingly demand SBOMs and documented controls from vendors.

talks.title: EL3vated Privileges: Glitching Google Wifi Pro From Root To EL3
talks.teaser: Cristofaro explores EL3vated Privileges: Glitching Google Wifi Pro From Root To EL3.
talks.summary:
Goal: root to EL3

Researchers use electromagnetic fault injection (EMFI) on Google Wifi Pro to escalate from compromised Linux root to ARM EL3—the highest secure-world privilege on TrustZone-based devices. The work continues a theme of relating energy perturbation to computing state at the hardware level.

Boot chain and storage access

The device boot flow runs ROM, signed secondary bootloader (SBL) at EL3, Qualcomm secure OS, U-Boot, then Android. By locating eMMC clock signals and removing a capacitor, they mounted internal flash in Linux, dumping 19 partitions including A/B SBL and U-Boot copies used for resilient updates.

Glitching path to EL3

With firmware dumped and boot stages mapped, EMFI targets critical verification or execution points to fault secure boot or trust-zone transitions. Achieving EL3 breaks assumptions that kernel compromise is the ceiling, showing consumer mesh routers still expose high-value silicon attack surfaces.
